question: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

Directive (EU) 2021/2167 requires credit purchasers and servicers to act in good faith, fairly and professionally and to provide borrowers with clear, non-misleading and specific information on the amounts owed. For the effective verification of a claim, it is crucial to be able to ascertain how it is structured, in particular as regards the capital, interest and other charges, and whether all payments made to the original creditor before the transfer have been taken into account. Accuracy and verifiability of data are particularly important when the claim is the basis for enforcement measures. The Commission is asked: 1.

Is it sufficient, under Article 10 of Directive (EU) 2021/2167, to disclose the total amount and its breakdown into capital, interest, fees and other charges, or must the information and calculations allowing full verification of the claim, including the full history of payments taken into account, be provided upon request?

Is it consistent with the obligations of good faith and fair dealing and transparency under Article 10 for a credit purchaser or servicer to continue with collection or enforcement actions where the borrower has requested but has not received the information necessary to verify the amount claimed?
If the directive does not guarantee a full right of verification before enforcement measures, does the Commission intend to propose its introduction?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.9.2026) Directive (EU) 2021/21671 (the Non-Performing Loans Directive (NPLD)) is a minimum harmonisation directive. The NPLD does not expressly entitle a borrower to obtain a complete payment history from the credit servicer/purchaser. It nevertheless requires the provision of certain information2 concerning the amounts due by the borrower, detailing what is due as capital, interests, fees and other permitted charges and a receipt or a letter of discharge for each payment received by a credit servicer3. Additional requirements may be set out under national legislation transposing the NPLD. The NPLD sets out requirements on how credit servicers/purchasers should act in their dealings with borrowers but does not provide for any automatic suspension of collection or enforcement of claims in the case of non-compliance. The responsibility for the assessment of the credit servicer/purchaser’s conduct against the requirements of good faith, fairness, professional diligence and transparency rests with national competent authorities. Under Articles 30 and 31 of the NPLD, the Commission is required to evaluate the functioning of the Directive and, where appropriate, consider whether further measures may be needed, including concerning communications with borrowers.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2021/2167/oj. 2 Article 10(2)(g) of Directive (EU) 2021/2167. 3 Article 6(2)(d) of Directive (EU) 2021/2167.
